item.title: Sebi extends digital accessibility compliance deadline to January 31
item.description: The requirements are part of Sebi's earlier circulars on mandatory compliance with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and the rules framed thereunder by all regulated entities ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: Sebi has extended the deadline for regulated entities to complete key digital accessibility compliance requirements to January 31 next year, following requests from market participants.In a circular dated October 30, Sebi said the extension covers the appointment of an International Association of Accessibility Professionals (IAAP) auditor, conducting accessibility audits of digital platforms and remediation of findings arising from the audits.The requirements are part of Sebi's earlier circulars on mandatory compliance with the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and the rules framed thereunder by all regulated entities.The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) said it had received representations from regulated entities seeking an extension for submitting their compliance status and had also reviewed the progress made by them.The circular refers to five earlier communications issued by the regulator in July, August, September and December 2025, and July 31, 2026, relating to digital accessibility requirements.The regulator said all other provisions of the earlier circulars will remain unchanged and must be complied with by regulated entities.The direction was issued to protect investors' interests, promote the development and regulate the securities market.

item.title: US jobs pickup may keep Federal Reserve on track to hike rates again
item.description: Forecasters expect the report to show monthly job growth more than doubled in October, to 65,000, while the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.2% ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Matthew Boesler and Craig Stirling Jobs week lies ahead for the US, which means a heavy slate of data ahead of the capstone monthly employment report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday.  Forecasters expect the report to show monthly job growth more than doubled in October, to 65,000, while the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.2%. That would leave the Federal Reserve on track for additional interest-rate increases in the months ahead to combat inflation.  Other labor-market data in the coming week could reinforce the stability theme. A monthly report on job openings due on Tuesday is expected to show listings ticked higher in September, and economists will also scrutinize numbers on layoffs and quitting. Weekly jobless claims figures out Thursday, meanwhile, are seen remaining near the lowest levels in decades.What Bloomberg Economics Says:“Underneath the steady unemployment rate, job losses are slowly climbing, but jobless claims don’t yet show mass layoffs building. The underlying story is that a low-hire, low-fire labor market is losing momentum, but not breaking.” —Anna Wong, Andrew Sacher and Eliza Winger Rounding out the US calendar are manufacturing figures on Monday, which are expected to show factory activity was robust again in October, and trade data on Wednesday which will probably confirm AI-related imports continued to push the trade deficit wider last month.  Then there’s a report on productivity on Thursday which forecasters expect to show a 2.6% boost in the third quarter, which would be the biggest in a year. Turning north, Canada also reports jobs numbers on Friday. Economists expect the unemployment rate to have remained roughly unchanged at 6.5% in October after Canada shed 68,300 jobs the previous month, pointing to a soft labor market.  Statistics Canada will also offer its first full-month assessment of how international trade has fared since talks between the US and Canada collapsed. A day earlier, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne will release the federal government’s budget, aimed at stimulating economic growth amid the ongoing trade rupture with the US. The government is expected to spend its fiscal windfall from high oil prices on tax measures to encourage investment, as well as programs aimed at improving affordability. The government intentionally scheduled the budget, titled Masters of Our Destiny, for after the US midterm elections.  Elsewhere, possible rate hikes from the UK to Australia, a closely watched post-election central-bank decision in Brazil, Asian purchasing manager indexes, and inflation data from key economies around Europe will be among the highlights.  Asia The first major piece of data is due on Sunday, when South Korea reports whether exports in October continued their high double-digit monthly growth. Shipments in September hit a record, and while economists expect a slowdown from that number they still forecast the value to exceed $110 billion in October.  On Monday, purchasing manager indexes are due from several countries, showing whether the strong factory performance seen so far this year continued into October. Central bank decisions will also be in focus in the coming week, with the Australian and Malaysian monetary authorities both setting rates.  The Reserve Bank of Australia on Tuesday is expected by most observers to hike again after inflation continued to get faster, while Malaysian policymakers are forecast to hold rates steady on Thursday. However, given the recent run of surprise decisions in Asia, the outcome of every meeting looks live at this point. Also on Thursday, the Bank of Japan will release minutes from its September meeting, when it hiked rates, and RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser is due to speak. On Saturday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda will give a speech in Washington DC. Monthly housing figures from Australia are due on Monday, with a decline in prices expected to continue across the country, while trade numbers on Thursday will show whether rising fuel costs and demand for chips and servers for new data centers continued to drive import growth in September. Hong Kong will announce third-quarter GDP on Tuesday, followed by Indonesia on Thursday. New Zealand on Wednesday is set to announce jobless and wages data for the third quarter, the final economic release before the national election on Saturday. Europe, West Asia, Africa The Bank of England is likely to raise its key rate for the first time in more than three years on Thursday, in a decision featuring a new round of forecasts.  With the energy-driven inflation shock persisting and Governor Andrew Bailey having warned recently that pressure to act is getting harder to resist, the move would align the UK with a tightening push across the Group of Seven.  Sweden’s Riksbank is also expected to act. Officials may hike their rate on Wednesday by a quarter point, to 2%, as a strengthening economy and continued war-related disruption to energy supplies increase the risk of inflation exceeding target. A reading of consumer prices comes out the following day.  Norway, with a benchmark already much higher at 4.5%, is anticipated to see no change. With core inflation steady at 3%, investors may focus on any Norges Bank comments signaling a hike in December that would bring borrowing costs there to the highest since the 2008 financial crisis. Turning to Eastern Europe, Poland’s Monetary Policy Council is anticipated to keep borrowing costs unchanged on Wednesday, but an escalating political spat that threatens to cripple the central bank may complicate the outlook. In Prague on Thursday, meanwhile, a Czech Republic rate hike is on the cards.  In the euro zone, where European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde just played down the danger of inflation spreading beyond energy, new data will signal if that’s still the case with the October reading of consumer prices on Wednesday.  The ECB’s wage tracker the following day may also draw attention, while the race to succeed Lagarde is likely to intensify now that she’s announced her plan to step down in February. Multiple appearances by policymakers are also on the calendar, including at a major conference on Thursday. Manufacturing data from some of the region’s biggest economies will also point to any momentum at the end of the third quarter. German factory orders come out on Thursday and industrial production on Friday, while numbers from France and Spain are due on those two days respectively.    Switzerland’s inflation release is scheduled for Tuesday, while Swiss National Bank President Martin Schlegel will speak two days later.   The same day, Turkey will publish inflation data, which is seen to have slowed to 29.5% in October. The central bank just lowered rates for the first time since January, to 36% from 37%, and said future cuts would be considered on a meeting-by-meeting basis. The South African Reserve Bank will hold its annual Market Practitioners Group conference on Tuesday. It will provide an update on the transition to the rand overnight index average, known as Zaronia, which replaces the Johannesburg interbank average rate at the end of this year. Finally, Zambia’s Finance Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane delivers his 2027 budget to lawmakers on Friday.  Latin America Peru on Sunday posts October consumer prices data for the capital city of Lima, and the consensus expects the annual print to accelerate from September’s 4.55% reading.  The central bank has been on hold at 4.25% since September 2025, but if last month’s inflation readings come in near estimates, the BCRP may have little choice but to tighten at its Nov. 12 meeting. In Colombia, the central bank’s quarterly monetary policy report will likely mark down growth estimates in light of August’s massive 7.4-magnitude earthquake, and possibly push up consumer price estimates as well. Separately, the minutes of the central bank’s Oct. 30 decision to deliver a hold at 12.25% amid signs of faltering growth will likely remain hawkish, with inflation still moving higher and expectations unanchored.  In Brazil, a sixth straight quarter-point rate reduction, putting the Selic at 13.5%, had looked to be a sure thing at the central bank’s Nov. 3-4 meeting. But Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s shock victory in the Oct. 25 election, giving him a fourth term, and the subsequent violent market selloff, upended the BCB’s policy outlook. Concern about currency weakness and no hint as to plans for getting government finances back in order has seen more than a few analysts and economists revise their forecast to a rate hold at 13.75%. Chile’s September activity report in the coming week is likely to leave little doubt that the economy shrank in the third quarter.  The minutes of the central bank’s October rate hold — borrowing costs were held at 4.5% for a seventh straight meeting — may tilt into hawkish terrain, while incoming inflation data may show an October rise of 4.6% against 4.1% in September, offering scant room for maneuver. In Mexico, the central bank will more than likely keep its key rate unchanged at 6.5% for a fourth straight meeting after annual inflation accelerated more than expected to move further above its 3% target.

Binance resumes crypto withdrawals after covering bulk of stolen $6.3 bn The heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea and analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts

Binance, which was founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP and dogecoin | Source: Bloomberg

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 3:01 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, resumed bitcoin, ether and some stablecoin withdrawals on Sunday and said others would follow in phases, after it covered 95% of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen from its platform.   The heist, which the FBI has tied to North Korea and analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.   Binance, which was founded in China, said the first phase of withdrawals would cover 15 crypto assets including bitcoin, ether, XRP and dogecoin. Bitcoin withdrawals resumed shortly after 0600 GMT, while ether, BNB and some USDT and USDC stablecoin withdrawals were also restored.

Binance said it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange.  FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT   The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Also Read

Explained: How hackers stole $6.3 bn in crypto from Binance in just 20 mins

Binance says it has covered $6 billion of $6.3 billion stolen in hack

North Korean hackers behind $6.3 billion Binance crypto heist, says FBI

Binance says 90% of assets stolen in record hack have been replenished

Binance's $6.3 bn hack signals the start of a risky era for crypto security

Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.   Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.

Analysts had also blamed North Korea for the heist.   The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.   US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday that the United States was still not certain if North Korea was involved.   "We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House account on X.  BINANCE VOWS TO BEAR FINANCIAL COSTS   Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located as of Friday, it said.

The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses.   The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance's $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.   Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that 50% of its SAFU funds would be used, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 billion.

Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.   Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack.   Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.  BINANCE FOUNDER CZ THANKS US LAW ENFORCEMENT   In a post on X that quoted the FBI statement on North Korea's involvement, Binance thanked the agency for its support. It did not respond to a request for comment on North Korea's involvement.

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who was convicted in the US of failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program before being pardoned by Trump last year, said US law enforcement agencies provided vital help, including by tracking and freezing the stolen assets.   "A tweet can't fully express our gratitude. Many crypto bros may not realize, a lot of the 'why bitcoin didn't drop more?' credit goes to them," Zhao wrote, referring to the US law enforcement agencies.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Germany protests: Shops looted in Frankfurt as Gen Z rallies turn violent

Germany protests: Shops looted in Frankfurt as Gen Z rallies turn violent Thousands demonstrated across Germany against rising living costs, cuts to public services and military service, before violence erupted in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg

Riot police officers stand in front of protesters during a demonstration organized by a group calling itself 'Gen Z Regelt' with the European Central Bank behind, in Frankfurt, Germany, on Saturday, October 31, 2026. (Photo: Bloomberg)

Rishabh Sharma New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 01 2026 | 1:42 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Shops were looted and clashes broke out between protesters and police across several German cities on Saturday, October 31, as largely peaceful demonstrations against the rising cost of living, public spending cuts and compulsory military service turned violent.   The unrest was reported in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, where police used water cannon to disperse demonstrators who allegedly attacked emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles, according to a BBC report.   Thousands of people had participated in demonstrations organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt, meaning "Gen Z takes charge", demanding greater investment in education and healthcare, improved public services and relief from rising living costs.

The violence in Germany coincided with similar youth-led demonstrations across Europe, including France, where more than 320,000 people took to the streets on Saturday.   What happened during the protests in Frankfurt?   Frankfurt, Germany's financial hub, witnessed some of the most serious violence as demonstrations escalated after nightfall. Also Read

Explained: How hackers stole $6.3 bn in crypto from Binance in just 20 mins

Fewer IIT, IIM alumni turn entrepreneurs despite rise in startup formation

2 foreign nationals die of suspected electrocution in Bengaluru hotel pool

EPFO exploring new investment options, including startups and AIF: Report

Police cordoned off a large section of the city's main shopping street after rioters smashed shop windows and looted several establishments.   Frankfurt police said violent riots were taking place in the city centre, prompting the deployment of special police units. Several shops were vandalised, while Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, according to the BBC report.

Police said several arrests had been made, although an exact figure was not immediately available.   Officials also reported that the windows of a gun shop had been smashed. Two weapons were seized following the arrest of a suspect. Other shops were reportedly broken into, with rioters stealing trainers and other merchandise.   Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, where Frankfurt is located, alleged that around 100 identified left-wing extremists had infiltrated the demonstration.   He described the violent conclusion to the protests as "shameful".   Why are Gen Z protesters demonstrating across Germany?   The demonstrations were organised by Gen Z regelt to draw attention to concerns about the affordability of living, inadequate funding for schools and healthcare, reductions in public spending and opposition to compulsory military service.

Lina Friedrich, a spokesperson for the campaign group, said the demonstrations were intended to promote peace and freedom rather than war and coercion, reported BBC .   She said the group's main priorities included better support for health and education systems, opposition to compulsory military service and a fairer distribution of financial burdens.   Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half the number estimated by organisers on their website.   German media, however, reported that tens of thousands of people had participated in demonstrations across the country.   Violence was also reported in other major German cities following largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day.

In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main railway station, with protesters throwing bottles and a bicycle.   In Berlin, a smaller evening demonstration following larger daytime protests resulted in injuries to 27 police officers, according to the city's police. Authorities said up to 56 people were temporarily detained during the unrest.   In Hamburg, protesters dressed in black reportedly set off fireworks and set barricades on fire. Public broadcaster NDR reported that 120 people had been arrested.   Protests across Europe   Youth-led demonstrations have recently taken place across several European countries, including France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania. Although the demands differ between countries, protesters have highlighted common concerns over rising living costs, access to affordable housing, the quality of education and reductions in public services.

In France, more than 320,000 people participated in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful demonstrations, particularly over living costs and public services, including education. Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, with tear gas used against demonstrators in some cities, according to the BBC .   Italy also witnessed demonstrations, with clashes reported between protesters and police in Rome and Turin.   In Portugal, police moved to dismantle a newly established tent camp after thousands of people marched against proposed rental legislation that demonstrators argued could worsen the country's housing crisis. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled over the past decade, adding to concerns about housing affordability.
